implementation_notes: C# puts optional named settings in the signature: optional parameters with defaults plus named arguments at the call site cover the common case, and object initializers (with `required` members since C# 11) cover larger option sets without a constructor per combination. Records with init-only properties and `with` expressions (C# 9) update a configuration non-destructively, and in DI-based .NET applications the Options pattern registers `Configure<TOptions>(Action<TOptions>)` delegates that apply configuration functions to a typed options object, including named options and validation. Option-function plumbing of the Go kind is only needed when the option set must stay closed and typed as a library contract.
pitfalls: Default parameter values are baked into the caller's compiled code: changing a default in a library does not change already-compiled callers, so defaults can silently diverge across assemblies after an upgrade (a documented .NET versioning trap).
Optional parameters must come last and gaps in the argument list can only be filled by name, so a mixed required/optional set forces callers to name every argument after the first skipped one.

Object initializers run after a parameterless constructor, so a partially initialized instance exists; prefer `required` members and init-only setters, and validate in the constructor so no half-built options object can be observed.
A mutable options class shared between callers lets one component change another's configuration; make options records/immutable or copy on entry.

variants.name: Record with init-only properties and with-expressions (C# 9)
variants.implementation_notes: A `record` with init-only properties makes the option set an immutable value: `new ServerOptions { Port = 9000 }` constructs it, `cfg with { Tls = true }` derives a modified copy without touching the original, and value equality makes configurations comparable and testable. The `with` expression calls the synthesized or hand-written copy constructor and then applies the member initializers, so copied instances stay valid; computed properties must be computed on access, or they keep values derived from the original instance.
pitfalls: `with` performs a shallow copy: reference-typed members are shared with the original, so mutable collections need a custom copy constructor or defensive copies.
Computed properties cached at initialization keep values derived from the original instance after a `with` (compute on access instead).
Init-only properties still cannot express an omitted component: a record constructor requires all positional components, so defaults must live in property initializers or a factory.

variants.name: Microsoft.Extensions.Options configuration delegates (library)
variants.implementation_notes: In DI-based .NET applications the options pattern treats the option set as a typed POCO configured by delegates: `services.Configure<ServerOptions>(o => o.Port = 9000)` registers `Action<ServerOptions>` configuration functions that run in registration order when the options object is first resolved (later configure delegates win per property unless a post-configure overrides), with named options, validation (`ValidateDataAnnotations`, `IValidateOptions<T>`) and reload support. It is the framework-scale realization of 'configuration functions over defaults': the option functions are registered rather than passed, and defaults live in the option type's property initializers.
pitfalls: Configuration delegates run once (IOptions) or per scope/snapshot (IOptionsSnapshot/IOptionsMonitor); resolving IOptions inside singletons freezes the values, so choose the interface by lifetime.
Registration order decides per-property overrides and there is no compiler check for a missing configuration, so a typo'd delegate silently leaves a default in place.
Options PoCo must have a public parameterless constructor and settable properties, which rules out records with required positional components unless configured via object initializers.
